text:
Sixty years have passed, yet whenever it rains, my thoughts always drift back to that little town that now exists only in memory. 
 
Back then, the streets were narrower, and there were no endless streams of traffic. Rainwater trickled gently from the eaves, leaving the old stone pavement glistening beneath the soft gray sky. Every morning, the bakery filled the air with the irresistible aroma of freshly baked bread. You could catch the scent of butter and warm flour from halfway down the street. Outside the barber shop, the familiar red, white, and blue striped pole turned slowly through the mist, while the owner of the general store knew everyone in town. He knew which child had stayed late after school and which elderly neighbor was feeling under the weather. 
 
Life was never wealthy, but it was honest, peaceful, and deeply fulfilling. 
 
The moment you pushed open the wooden door of the little café, a tiny bell would ring overhead, and the owner would greet you with a warm smile and a simple, "Good to see you." Outside, the rain fell quietly. Inside, golden light spilled across wooden tables, where a cup of hot coffee and a slice of apple pie were enough to make an afternoon feel complete. People didn't lower their heads to stare at glowing screens. They looked into each other's eyes, sharing stories about their families, the harvest, their children, and the quiet hopes they carried for tomorrow. 
 
I still remember those old automobiles parked along the roadside. They lacked the sleek lines of today's cars, but they carried the laughter of entire families. I remember the umbrella resting on a park bench, damp from the rain, as though its owner had only stepped away for a moment and would soon return. The gentle drizzle wrapped the whole town in a soft veil of light and shadow, quietly preserving our youth within the passing years. 
 
Today, that little town can no longer be found. 
 
The world has become faster. Buildings rise higher, city lights shine brighter, yet somehow people have grown farther apart. In those days, a family business could remain open for generations. Everyone on the same street knew one another, and a simple smile or friendly greeting was enough to brighten an entire day. Now many of those old shops have disappeared, familiar faces have grown old, and the people we once saw every day have scattered across the world. 
 
Yet memories never grow old. 
 
Whenever I see rain falling on a quiet street, warm light glowing through a shop window, or hear the gentle ring of a restaurant doorbell, I feel as though I have returned to those cherished days. I can almost smell the fresh bread once more. The coffee still seems to steam gently before me. The old cars still wait patiently by the curb. What once seemed like the most ordinary moments of everyday life have become treasures beyond measure—moments that can never be relived. 
 
Only with the passing of time do we come to understand that the greatest memories are not born from extraordinary events, but from the ordinary days we once believed would last forever. They remain hidden within the sound of falling rain, the glow of a single lamp, the warmth of a neighborhood café, and the quiet corners of our hearts. As our hair turns gray, we realize that what we truly long for is not merely that little town, but a way of life that moved more slowly, where neighbors cared for one another, and where every new day was greeted with hope.
